installs the title screen's fade interrupt: blanks the display, black border and background, stops CIA 1's timer A, points $0314 at $0E6A, asks for line 0 and turns the raster interrupt on. Called from the title screen builder at $1024.

the title screen's raster interrupt: a fade worked by rewriting colour memory. $1012 says which phase it is in (0 fade in, 2 fade out, 3 hold, 1 and 4 idle), $1011 the step inside it, 0 to 9. Each step takes four colours from the tables at $0FE5, $0FEF, $0FF9 and $1003, puts them in $100D to $1010 and calls $0EF9 to paint the four bands of the screen with them. The fade in counts up to 10 and goes to the hold, the hold counts $1013 to 256 and starts the fade out, the fade out counts down to 0 and stops. It then calls the music at $1947 and ends through the KERNAL's handler at $EA31.
writes the four colours in $100D to $1010 into the four bands of colour memory the title screen uses, forty cells each, so one call recolours the whole picture. Called by both halves of the fade.

counts frames 0, 1, 2 so the driver only acts on every third one

the music, one tick at a time, called once a frame from the title and plaque interrupts. It does nothing on two frames in three, so the tune runs at about 16.7 ticks a second on a PAL machine. On the third it serves each of the three voices in turn: it counts the voice's note down, and when that runs out takes the next note number from the voice's own stream ($15E2, $1680 or $1768), looks the number up in the three note tables to get the frequency high byte, the low byte and the length, writes the frequency and the waveform to that voice, and steps the stream on. A note number of $FF ends the tune, and the driver starts all three streams again from the beginning, so the music is endless.

the floor-select screen's own loop. It marks the floor the player is on to begin with, taken from $02A7, then waits: up and down move the marker, wrapping round the four floors, and each move rubs out the old marker and draws the new one at column 32 of the floor's row. Fire returns the chosen floor in A. Between repeats it idles for about a fiftieth of a second and then waits for raster line $F0, so the marker steps at a readable pace.
the pause between two steps of the floor marker: a counted loop and then a wait for raster line $F0, which is what stops one push running through all four floors
"SELECT MISSION", ASCII ending $00
builds the mission-select screen - clears colour memory, single-colour text from the character set at $2800 - draws "SELECT MISSION" and the number, and then waits in $1D99

the mission-select screen's loop: up steps the mission number on, down steps it back, each wrapping round 1 to 4 and redrawing the digit, and fire shows the briefing at $1E3F and returns the chosen mission in A. Between steps it idles about a quarter of a second.
draws the mission number at row 10, column 18. The digit shown is five minus $0836, so the number on the screen counts the other way from the number the game keeps: the screen's 1 is $0836 = 4.
steps $0836 on by one, wrapping from 4 back to 1, and redraws the digit
steps $0836 back by one, wrapping from 1 round to 4, and redraws the digit
"MISSION", the heading of the mission briefing
the second line of the briefing's heading, ASCII ending $00
"RESCUE THE PRISONER"
"BLOW UP THE CASTLE"

the briefing the mission select shows when fire is pressed: clears the screen, draws "MISSION", the number and then one of the two orders - "BLOW UP THE CASTLE" when $0836 is 4, "RESCUE THE PRISONER" otherwise - and holds it for about three seconds. Because the digit drawn is five minus $0836, the screen that reads MISSION 1 is the one that orders the castle blown up.
holds the finished briefing on screen for about three seconds before play begins
"WELL DONE !"
"YOUR MISSION WAS A" and, after it, "SUCCESS"
"SUCCESS", ASCII ending $00, the last line of the end-of-mission screen

the screen that follows a mission the player finished: blanks the display, puts the screen back on the big alphabet's character set at $2800 in single-colour text, clears colour memory and draws "WELL DONE !", "YOUR MISSION WAS A" and "SUCCESS", each in its own place

the play screen's character set, 256 tiles of eight bytes. It holds the castle's walls, floors, doors, furniture, the figures, the pickups, the status panel's frame, the ten letters the panel needs and the digits at $F0 to $F9. facts.md has the letters' codes.
the four tiles a box of ammunition is drawn from, which the supplies screen borrows
the four tiles a door key is drawn from, which the supplies screen borrows
the eight tiles a painting is drawn from, which the valuables screen borrows
the eight tiles a vase is drawn from, which the valuables screen borrows
the eight tiles a plate of cold food is drawn from, which the supplies screen borrows
more of the play screen's character set, the tiles from $20
more of the play screen's character set, the tiles from $28
more of the play screen's character set: the tiles from $30, which hold the walls and the doors
more of the play screen's character set, the tiles from $66, which draw the pile of jewels
more of the play screen's character set, the tiles from $6E
the upper half of the play screen's character set, tiles $80 to $FF, which hold the panel's frame and the digits
the sixteen tiles of the play character set the prisoner is drawn with, rewritten from $F000 every time he moves
more of the play screen's character set, the tiles from $DC

the character set the attract screens and the message line are written in. Each character of text is a block of two cells by two, so one letter takes four of these, and the code of its first cell is the ASCII value masked to six bits and multiplied by four.
the upper half of the big alphabet, which holds the digits, the punctuation and the sixteen cells the attract screens borrow for the item pictures at $2F40
the sixteen tiles of the attract screens' character set that the supplies and valuables screens overwrite with pictures copied out of the play screen's set
the first item picture the attract screens copy into the big alphabet's spare codes
the second item picture the attract screens copy there
part of an item picture the supplies screen copies into the big alphabet's spare codes
part of an item picture the supplies screen copies there
the third item picture the attract screens copy there
the top half of the fourth supply's picture, copied here out of the play character set
the bottom half of the fourth supply's picture, copied here out of the play character set
the fourth item picture the attract screens copy there

the sprite shapes, 64 bytes each, which the pointers at $07F8 name as a number from $C0. The player's four are $C0 to $C3, and $E0 to $EF are the four he is drawn with for each of the four directions.
more sprite shapes, the numbers from $C4
more sprite shapes, the numbers from $C5
more sprite shapes, numbers $D0 to $DF
more sprite shapes, numbers $E0 to $EF, the player facing each of the four ways
the last sprite shapes, numbers $F0 to $F6: the castle emblem in the panel and the bullet, one shape for each direction it can fly
the three bytes the mission select jumps to, which go straight on to the game's cold start at $4016
where the key count waits while the mission screens are up; $404F copies it back into $02AC when the next mission in the same castle begins
where the ammunition waits between two missions of the same castle
where the hit count waits between two missions of the same castle
where the score's top two digits wait between two missions of the same castle
where the score's middle two digits wait between missions
where the score's bottom two digits wait between missions
the mission the player picked on the select screen, 1 to 4 as the game counts them
which floor the mission's prisoner is on, or $FF on the demolition mission, which has none. The room builder compares it with the floor the player is on.
set while the player has just come out of the lift, so the next mission starts him at the lift rather than in the storage room
set when the prisoner is in the part of the castle being built, so $4151 puts the prisoner into the room instead of leaving the slot empty
jump stub into the message printer at $592E, which the prisoner's own code calls

the game's own first code, reached from the mission select. Clears the sixteen icon characters the attract screens borrowed at $2F40, blacks the border and background, clears the mission-in-progress flag and the counters of what the player is carrying, sets the score to six ASCII zeros, and goes to $4946, the top of the game's own loop.

sets a mission going: puts the character set back, clears the game's variables at $02A8 to $02FF, and when a mission has already been played in this castle restores the ammunition, hits, keys and carried items the player ended it with. Then it builds the room ($601B), the panel ($5F9E) and starts the game's interrupt ($4BF2), and waits for the interrupt to report itself running.

sets the eight sprites up for play: no expansion, multicolour for the lower four, the bullet yellow, the screen at $0400 with the play character set at $2000, multicolour text with the two extra backgrounds, and the three sprites of the castle emblem parked in the panel at fixed places. It then puts the player's four sprites round the player's position in $02DF and $02E0: sprites 0 and 2 on the left, 1 and 3 eight pixels further right, 0 and 1 on the top row, 2 and 3 a row of 21 lines below.
blanks the four sprite shapes the player is drawn with, writing zero into both halves of each of the four 64-byte blocks at once through the pointer in $FC

fills all four pages of the screen with the solid black tile $EF and clears colour memory, then points the sprites at their shapes - $C0 to $C3 for the player's four, $F0 to $F2 for the castle emblem in the panel - and colours the panel's two bottom rows

finishes setting the mission up: draws the status panel ($5DC8), clears the message line ($5995), and on the first mission of a castle shows the greeting "WELCOME TO THE EAGLES NEST." from $5694. It then draws the room ($47F1), tells the interrupt to start ($4BF1 = 1), turns all eight sprites on and waits for the interrupt to report back.

the last of the setup: colours the player's four sprites, marks the mission as under way, sets the two shared sprite colours, starts the room's movers ($5ABD) and drops into the game's main loop at $484A
set once a mission has started, so the next mission restores what the player was carrying instead of starting fresh

the player's part of each frame. The low three bits of $02AA say what is going on: 1, 2, 3 or 4 means a room change is in progress and the matching scroll runs a step of it ($432E up, $43D6 down, $4480 left, $4528 right); with none of them set the player takes an ordinary turn at $4297.

the player's turn, once a frame. It works out which tiles are round the player ($5C46), holds everything until fire is let go when $02E3 says a shot is pending, and then counts $02BA up to 3 and acts only on the fourth frame, which is why the player steps one tile every four frames. On that frame it reads control port 2 and goes to the routine for the direction pushed: up $42E2, down $438A, left $4434, right $44DC.

moves the player up a tile when nothing solid is in the way. The four tiles round the player, which $5C46 left in $5C23 to $5C26, must all be below $2D: a tile code of $2D or more is a wall, a door or furniture and stops the move. Otherwise it takes 8 from the player's y, clears the standing-still count, and flips the walking frame. At y = $62 the player is at the top edge of the room, so instead it asks for the room above by setting bits in $02AA.
moves the player down a tile when the four tiles at $5C41 to $5C44 are all below $2D. At y = $B2 the player is at the bottom edge, so it asks for the room below instead by setting bits in $02AA.

moves the picture one row at a time while the player crosses between two rooms up or down, 13 steps counted in $FF. Each step moves the room pointer in $FA on by 128 bytes, takes 8 off the player's y, and brings each shot in the air with it, so a bullet keeps its place in the room rather than on the screen. The last step clears the direction bits in $02AA and leaves only the flag that says a room change is under way.
moves the player left a tile when the four tiles at $5C28, $5C2E and their neighbours are all below $2D, and sets the facing to 3. At the left edge it asks for the room to the left instead.

moves the picture one column at a time while the player crosses into the room on the left, counted down in $FE. Each step moves the room pointer in $FA back a byte, adds 8 to the player's x, and brings each shot in the air with it.

moves the player right a tile when the four tiles at $5C2D, $5C33, $5C39 and $5C3F are all below $2D, and sets the facing to 4. At x = $B0 the player is at the right edge, so it asks for the room to the right instead.

moves the picture one column at a time while the player crosses into the room on the right, counted up in $FE to $64. The mirror of $4480: the room pointer goes on a byte, the player's x comes back 8, and the shots in the air come with it.
takes a shot out of the air once it has turned back at a room's edge, which is what bits 1 and 5 of $02AF mark, and then runs whatever is still flying ($4692)

fire. It moves the shots already in the air ($4692) and then, if fire is held and this is a fresh press, fires one. The player can have two shots in the air at once: the first is fired when neither is, the second once the first has travelled 8 pixels. With no rounds left it says "OUT OF AMMO!"; otherwise it takes one off the ammunition in decimal mode, redraws the count, points the player's sprites the right way ($46A5), and starts the shot from the player's own position offset by the tables at $4699 and $469D, with five tiles of range.

fires the player's second shot, once the first has travelled at least 8 pixels and no second one is already in the air. It spends a round, points the sprites, and starts the shot at the player with five tiles of range.
moves each of the player's two shots along, one step a frame
how far across the player the shot starts, one byte for each of the four directions
how far down the player the shot starts, one byte for each of the four directions
the first of the player's four sprite shapes for each direction faced: $E0 up, $E4 down, $E8 left, $EC right

points the player's four sprites at the shapes for the way the player is facing, from the table at $46A1, marks a shot as pending, and gives the bullet sprite the shape for that direction, $F3 plus the direction less one
how the bullet sprite is being handled this frame; the interrupt reads it when it places sprite 4
where the bullet sprite sits beside the player for each direction
where the bullet sprite sits below the player for each direction

moves the player's first shot one tile in its direction, if one is in the air. At the edge of the room ($3A at the top, $E2 at the bottom, $20 at the left, $F2 at the right) it flips bit 1 of $02AF instead of going on.
moves the player's second shot one tile in its direction, the same way as $46FA does the first, and counts its distance in $02B4
how many rows of the room are left to draw, counted down from 20

draws the whole room, 28 tiles across and 21 rows down, from the castle map the pointer in $FA names. It is written as a self-modifying loop: the bytes at $4815, $4818 and $481E are the operands of the three instructions in the inner loop, holding the map address, the screen address and the colour address, and the routine rewrites them as it goes. Each tile code goes to the screen and the colour the tile colour table at $8600 gives it goes to colour memory. A row of the map is 128 bytes, so each row adds $80 to the source and 40 to the two destinations.
the operand of the instruction that reads the map: the address of the row being drawn
the high byte of the map address the room drawer reads, which it rewrites a row at a time
the operand of the instruction that writes the screen
the high byte of the screen address the room drawer writes, which it rewrites a row at a time
the operand of the instruction that writes colour memory
the rest of the room drawer's inner loop, whose operands $47F1 rewrites. The address $481F itself is the operand that holds where in colour memory the row being drawn goes.

hands the machine over to the game: points $0314 at the game's own interrupt at $4AA7, stops CIA 1's timer A, asks for a raster interrupt on line $E9, banks BASIC out and leaves the KERNAL and the I/O in ($01 = $36), and drops into the loop at $4871

the game's main loop, which does nothing itself but watch four things and hand over when one of them happens. $02D3 = $FF means the mission is over ($48F0), $02C8 = 2 that the player is dead ($48D4), $02E9 = 1 that the player has stepped into the lift ($49EC) and 2 that a prisoner has been brought home ($4A5C), and $C5 = $10 that SPACE is down, which pauses. Everything else - the player, the guards, the shots, the panel - is done by the interrupt.

SPACE pauses. It sets the pause flag, waits for SPACE to be let go, and then holds the game: with nothing on the joystick and the message line idle it prints "...PAUSING...", and it keeps printing it until SPACE or the stick is touched, when it clears the flag and the loop goes on.
the player is dead: puts the I/O banking back, pauses the game while the message line empties, turns every sprite off, and goes back to the top of the game at $4946 through $6018
the mission's job is done: pauses the game, clears the message line and waits for it to empty, then goes on to the end-of-mission screens

what happens between missions. Puts the KERNAL's own interrupt back and starts CIA 1's timer A again, so the mission screens have a working keyboard. With no mission in progress it clears the castle flag and asks for a mission ($1D23): mission 1 puts the prisoner in the basement, 2 on the first floor, 3 on the second, and 4, the demolition, has no prisoner, which is $FF in $4010. With a mission already in progress it asks which floor the lift should go to ($1AB2) instead, and keeps the keys, the ammunition, the hits and the three digits of the score in $4009 to $400E while the screens are up.
the player has stepped onto the lift: puts the I/O banking back, holds the game while the message line empties, forgets this floor's state and goes back to $4946, which asks which floor to ride to
which of the game's two interrupt bands comes next, flipped between 1 and 0 each time

the game's own interrupt, and where nearly everything in play happens. It serves two bands, flipped by $4AA6: one sets the screen to the play character set at $2000 and does the game's work ($4ACD), then asks for line $E3; the other sets the message line's character set at $2800 with its fine scroll and draws the sprites ($4B4C), then asks for line $FC. It never chains to the KERNAL's handler, so the jiffy clock and the KERNAL's keyboard scan do not run while the game is playing, which is why the game scans SPACE itself.

the interrupt's first band. Puts the screen on the play character set at $2000 in multicolour with 38 columns, keeps the room's movers going ($5AA0), scans SPACE, and then, unless the game is paused or a room change is under way, works through a three-phase rota counted in $02EF: two phases redraw the room ($47F1), the third does the guards, the pickups and the collisions ($4D3A, $5212, $4586, $5A33, $5B1B, $5CB9, $5F27). It ends by stepping the message line's scroll four pixels and shifting the text along when that wraps.
steps the message line four pixels left, and when that has used up a whole character shifts the line's text along ($4BDC) and brings the next character in ($5951)

the interrupt's second band. Puts the screen on the big alphabet at $2800 with the message line's fine scroll in $D016, paints the panel ($600C), draws the room's movers ($5BBA), lets the bullet sprite fade after a hit, runs the player and the room changes ($426F) unless a change is already under way, and places the player's four sprites and the bullet's round the positions in $02DF and $02E0.
the bytes before the wipe interrupt's own code, which nothing reaches
shifts the message line's two rows one cell to the left, so the text moves on after the fine scroll has used up a whole cell
the raster line the wipe's open band starts at
the raster line the wipe's open band ends at
which of the wipe interrupt's two bands comes next, flipped each time
how far the mission's opening has got: the main code sets 1 to ask for the wipe to close, and the interrupt answers 2 when it has closed and 3 when it has opened again
installs the interrupt that wipes the screen open and shut between missions: stops CIA 1's timer A, sets the band to lines $32 to $FA and points $0314 at $4C22

the interrupt that opens and shuts the screen. Its two bands set the display on inside the band and an invalid, black mode outside it, so what shows is a window that closes to the middle of the screen and opens again four lines at a time. It reports where it has got to in $4BF1.

the band outside the window: an invalid video mode, which the chip draws as black, and the player's sprites turned black with it. It is also where the window's two lines are moved, four at a time, towards the middle of the screen and back out again.
the band inside the window: ordinary multicolour text and the player's sprites in their own colours

fades the room in. It copies the whole play character set out to $8000 and clears it, so every tile is blank, then copies it back through a mask that grows a bit at a time - 1, 3, 7 and so on - so the tiles appear a plane at a time. $02AB is the mask.
the places in the tile grid the walked-onto test looks at, which it steps through skipping the grid's right-hand column

looks through the tile grid for anything the player has walked onto, skipping the grid's right-hand column. A door key is counted and named, a painting, a vase, cold food, a pendant, first aid and a lift pass are each picked up by their own routine, and a chest found anywhere but the first five places of the grid gives ammunition.
the player walked onto a door key: counts it in decimal mode, says "YOU HAVE FOUND" and "A DOOR KEY.", and clears its two tiles
writes the six-by-six grid of tiles back into the castle map, so that whatever a pickup or a shot changed in the grid reaches the map and then the screen
the player walked onto a painting: says "YOU HAVE FOUND", puts 25 points in the queue, which the ticker turns into 2500, and falls into the shared tail that names it
clears the painting from the map, says "A PAINTING." and redraws the room's tiles
the player walked onto a vase: "YOU HAVE FOUND" and 15 waiting points, which is 1500
clears the vase from the map, says "A VASE." and redraws
the player walked onto cold food: "YOU HAVE FOUND", and takes $10 off the hits in decimal mode, stopping at none
clears the food from the map, says "SOME COLD FOOD." and redraws
the player walked onto a pendant: "YOU HAVE FOUND" and 40 waiting points, which is 4000
clears the pendant from the map, says "A PENDANT." and redraws

the player walked onto a chest of ammunition. It clears the chest's two tiles and adds $10 to the ammunition in decimal mode, which is sixteen rounds; if that would carry past 99 it sets 99 instead and says "ANY MORE AMMO WOULD BE WASTED !".
the part of the ammunition pickup that runs when the count would carry past 99: it sets 99 and says "ANY MORE AMMO WOULD BE WASTED !"
the player walked onto first aid: "YOU HAVE FOUND", and clears the hits altogether
works back from the place in the tile grid to the map address of the object's own corner, clears its five tiles, scores it, redraws the room and says "FIRST AID."
the player walked onto a lift pass: "YOU HAVE FOUND", clears it from the grid, says "A LIFT PASS." and marks the pass as carried
rubs an object out of the tile grid, which the redraw then takes to the screen

works out where in the castle map a place on the screen is. The room's top left corner is x = $20, y = $3A, a tile is eight pixels square and a row of the map is 128 bytes, so the address is the room pointer in $FA plus 16 times the pixels down plus an eighth of the pixels across. It leaves the address in $02 and $03.

looks up the map tile each shot in the air has reached. Tiles $3E and $3F and the codes below $08 are air, so the shot flies on; anything else stops it. On a hit the shot is taken out of the air, its direction is kept in $02D2 and $529B decides what was hit.

decides what a shot hit, by the tile code. $76 to $C0 and $D4 to $E3 are the soldiers and officers, $30 to $3E and $C0 to $CB and $E7 to $EE are walls that just stop it, $5E to $6D a soldier that falls, $49 and $4A the two halves of a steel door, $47 and $48 a wooden door, $43 to $46 a mirror that shortens the shot's range to three, $40 to $FB the furniture, and anything else is looked for in the six-by-six grid around the shot, where the nine places listed at $5374 are checked for the code of a pickup.
the nine places in the six-by-six tile grid a shot looks at to find what it hit, since an object is drawn from several tiles and only its first one names it
a shot has set a detonator off: marks this floor's charge as armed in $5F9A plus the floor, says "DETONATOR ACTIVATED.", and scores it
the shot hit something that is no use: says "YOU ARE WAISTING AMMO." (the game's own spelling) and leaves the shot's range at two
a shot hit an open chest, which breaks what is in it: clears the two tiles of the chest and scores it
the shot hit a painting, which is picked up all the same: says "YOU HAVE SHOT", and $4ECD names it and clears it
the shot hit cold food; $4F27 names it and clears it
the shot hit a pendant; $4F51 names it and clears it
the shot hit a vase; $4EF7 names it and clears it
the shot hit first aid; $4FA5 names it and clears it
the shot hit one of the four pieces of furniture, codes $4C to $4F, and turns it into the broken shape $50 to $53, two tiles on the top row and two on the row below
the shot hit a lift pass, which is no use at all: "SHOOTING A LIFT PASS IS A BIT SILLY !"
a shot hit the right half of a steel door, code $49: sets the door's state and opens it from $50F7
a shot hit the left half of a steel door, code $4A, and opens it the same way
a shot hit the lower half of a wooden door, code $47, which can be shot open: $5192 does it
a shot hit the upper half of a wooden door, code $48; the same as $54F3 with the map address moved up a row

a shot hit a soldier or an officer, codes $5E to $6D. The twelve codes are the three shapes each of four kinds, and each kind takes the shot in its own place: the tile hit is moved left, right, up or down to find the figure's own square before it is knocked down.
the game's 33 messages for the line at the bottom of the screen, ASCII, each ending "@" ($40); facts.md lists them
how far the message line's scroll has read into the buffer at $8800
how far the printer has filled the buffer; the line is idle when the two are equal
which half of the character now entering the line is showing, because a character of the big alphabet is two cells wide and the line brings one cell in at a time

puts a message in the queue for the line at the bottom of the screen. $FC and $FD point at the text, which is ASCII ending "@". It copies the characters into the buffer at $8800, masking each to six bits as the big alphabet needs, adds a space after the last, and leaves the write position in $592C. The line is only emptied by the scroll, so a routine that wants to wait for the message to finish watches $592B against $592C.

brings the next cell of the message into the right-hand end of the line, at $07BF and $07E7. A character takes two turns, its left half and then its right, after which the read position moves on. With nothing left to show it puts a space there instead.

writes every number on the status panel: the keys at row 4, the ammunition at row 6, the hits at row 8 and the six digits of the score at row 11, each as two screen codes from $5A20. On the way it also works out where the player is in the castle, in tiles, and leaves it in $02CA and $02CB.

turns one binary-coded-decimal byte into the two screen codes that print it. The play character set keeps its digits at $F0 to $F9, so each nibble only has to be ORed with $F0; the upper one is shifted down first. Every number on the panel goes through here.

the game's prodding. $02C1 counts up to $80 and then, if the player has not moved, counts $02BF; at fourteen of those it says "COME ON ! GET ON WITH IT.....". Holding fire without moving counts $02C0 instead, and at seven it says "LETS GET DOWN TO SOME SERIOUS DESTRUCTION !". Any movement puts both counts back to nothing.

adds the points waiting in $02C5 to the score, one a frame, so the number on the panel climbs rather than jumps. Each one adds 1 to the score's middle pair of digits in decimal mode, carrying into the top pair, so one waiting point is a hundred on the panel; the bottom pair is never written, which is why every score in this game ends in two zeros.
says which floor the mission starts on: "YOU ARE" and then one of "IN THE BASEMENT.", "ON THE GROUND FLOOR.", "ON THE FIRST FLOOR." or "ON THE SECOND FLOOR."
the first four of the sixteen tiles the player's square is covering, kept while tile $55 stands in for him
the second four of them
the third four of them
the last four of them

writes the player into the castle map so that the figures can see him. It stamps tile $55 over the sixteen tiles the player's square covers, keeping what was there in the four buffers at $5B0B, $5B0F, $5B13 and $5B17, then runs the figures and the prisoner, and puts the sixteen tiles back. The figures only ever test whether the tile ahead is empty, so this is how walking into the player is noticed at all.

watched each frame. While $02D3 is 0 it reads the hits: at $50, that is fifty, the mission is over and the player is dead. $FF means the mission is already over and the screen goes black. Anything between 1 and $11 is a step of the explosion that ends the demolition mission, which walks through the seventeen colours at $5C11 and repeats five times.
the seventeen border and background colours the castle's explosion flashes through, in order
the six-by-six block of map tiles around the player or another mover, read by $5C55. The movement tests read the four of them the player's own square covers.
the four tile codes the player's own square overlaps, worked out each frame by $5C46; every one must be below $2D for a move to be allowed
the second of the four tiles the player's own square overlaps
the third of them
the fourth of them
the last two tiles of the grid's first row
the second row of the six-by-six tile grid around the player
the right-hand tile of the grid's second row, which the move to the right tests
the third row of the grid
the right-hand tile of the grid's third row
the fourth row of the grid
the right-hand tile of the grid's fourth row
the fifth row of the grid
the right-hand tile of the grid's fifth row
the grid's sixth row
the second tile of the grid's sixth row, which the move down tests
the third tile of the grid's sixth row
the fourth tile of the grid's sixth row
the last two tiles of the six-by-six grid around the player
works out which tiles surround the player, from the position in $02DF and $02E0, by way of $51CD and $5C55, and leaves them in the grid at $5C22

reads the six-by-six block of map tiles around the place the pointer in $06 names into the grid at $5C22, six bytes a row. A row of the map is 128 bytes away, which the routine reaches by setting bit 7 of Y and stepping the pointer's high byte, so it never needs a second pointer.
the sixteen places in the tile grid the jewels are looked for in

the pile of jewels, which is four tiles, $66 to $69. It looks round the player for any of them, works back to the pile's own corner, queues 40 points, which the ticker turns into 4000, says "YOU HAVE FOUND" and "SOME JEWELS.", and clears it.

draws the status panel: its frame down the right of the screen, the three labels KEYS, AMMO and HITS placed cell by cell from the ten letters the play character set holds, the box round each number, and the colours of every part.
